title: Reading the evidence
summary: Selected research on spirituality and mental health. Read findings alongside study design and limits of inference.
rawText: Reading the evidence Selected research on spirituality and mental health. Read findings alongside study design and limits of inference. What are we measuring? Spirituality, religiosity, meaning and wellbeing are different constructs. When a spirituality measure incorporates wellbeing, its association with mental health may partly reflect conceptual overlap. Examine definitions and item content before interpreting a coefficient. Association, change and treatment effects Cross-sectional associations do not establish temporal order. Cohorts improve temporal information but cannot remove all confounding. In randomized trials, comparator choice and attrition matter. A nonsignificant overall difference in the religious CBT trial does not establish equivalence. Support, struggles and possible harm Belief and community may offer support or involve guilt, exclusion and conflict. Do not collapse positive and negative coping into one score. Spiritual struggle alone is not a disorder. Nonbelief is neither a deficit nor a mental illness. Culture and life stage An association in one country, age group or religious tradition does not automatically transfer to another. Adolescence raises questions about family context, while later life brings loss and social support into focus. Who is absent from the sample matters alongside the average association. Disaster, grief and boundaries of care Professional accounts after disasters help identify needs and service contexts. They do not show that an intervention reduces trauma symptoms. Spiritual support should follow the person’s wishes, avoid imposed meanings of loss and preserve access to needed mental health care. From evidence to professional practice A research association alone does not justify introducing spirituality into a client’s care. Consider preferences, informed consent, professional competence and the intervention’s purpose together. Professional guidance offers an ethical framework. Claims of treatment benefit require controlled evidence. Why longitudinal findings differ The link between attendance and later mental health cannot be reduced to one coefficient. US cohorts report some favourable associations, UK within-person analyses are mostly nonsignificant, and ALSPAC results are small or compatible with zero. Brazilian medical students show some favourable associations with organisational religiosity. These are not replications in an identical population. Distinguish between-person differences, within-person change, outcomes and follow-up periods. Counting positive and negative studies cannot establish an overall benefit or harm. Spiritual harm and clinical context Spiritual harm after clergy abuse and religious coping in psychosis are distinct research questions. The scoping review maps a limited, heterogeneous literature rather than treatment efficacy. The psychosis review examines associations between forms of coping and clinical outcomes. Neither should be presented as an explanation of the other. Avoid pathologising religious identity while also recognising adverse experiences. Research findings do not replace consent, client preferences or professional competence boundaries.

title: Reading a study through its evidence
summary: A working guide to connect the question, design, sample, measurement and findings in one record.
rawText: Reading a study through its evidence A working guide to connect the question, design, sample, measurement and findings in one record.  Start with what the study tests Record the question, design, sample, country, setting and follow-up separately. Spirituality, religiosity, religious coping, integration preference and practice should not be entered as interchangeable constructs. Identify the instrument, respondent and measurement time for each variable. Record findings with their limits Record the comparator, main outcome, reported effect size and confidence interval. When only an abstract is available, do not infer missing methods. Do not label a cross-sectional association a causal effect. Examine selection bias, missing data, cultural context, funding and conflicts of interest separately. Separate a study from a synthesis A review additionally needs its scope, search date, information sources, eligibility criteria and selection decisions documented. PRISMA guides reporting, not a standalone quality score. The template here supports extraction. It is not a completed review or a risk-of-bias instrument.

title: Spiritual experience and counseling
summary: A starting point for understanding the person’s experience, meaning and preferences before turning to concepts.
rawText: Spiritual experience and counseling A starting point for understanding the person’s experience, meaning and preferences before turning to concepts. Start with the person’s language Faith, belonging, conscience or the meaning of life may arise in a conversation. None automatically establishes a spiritual need. Our proposed starting point is to ask what the person means in their own words. Requiring the label “spirituality” and imposing that label are two different ways of narrowing the conversation. Discussion is not consent to a practice Sharing a topic is not the same as requesting a religious practice or the practitioner’s interpretation. Someone may want to describe prayer without wanting to pray together during a session. title: ASERVIC 2025: three areas of practice for spiritual and religious issues
summary: A brief reading on how ASERVIC’s 2009 competencies were reorganised as best practices in 2025.
rawText: ASERVIC 2025: three areas of practice for spiritual and religious issues A brief reading on how ASERVIC’s 2009 competencies were reorganised as best practices in 2025. From competencies to best practices The spiritual and religious competencies ASERVIC published in 2009 comprise 14 items in six categories. The 2025 version reorganises them as best practices. The new arrangement draws on Cheston’s Ways Paradigm and groups 20 practices under three headings: ways of being, ways of understanding and ways of intervening. The document presents them not as goals reached once, but as areas that develop across a professional lifetime. Ways of being: the counselor’s own stance The four practices under the first heading concern the counselor’s self-awareness. Counselors are expected to keep examining their own beliefs and values and to evaluate how these affect the counseling process. They are also expected to recognise the limits of their understanding of the person’s spiritual and religious perspective. Supervision or consultation is recommended when countertransference or moral incongruence arises. Ways of understanding: knowledge and assessment The seven practices under the second heading concern knowledge and assessment. They include being able to describe the similarities and differences between spirituality and religion, and having access to resources on various belief systems, agnosticism and atheism. Accordingly, counselors are expected to use models of spiritual and religious development and to assess the person’s perspective from intake onwards. With client consent, consultation with religious or spiritual leaders may form part of this assessment. Ways of intervening: carrying it into practice The nine practices under the third heading concern carrying the first two areas into counseling. Their foundation is responding to what the client says about spirituality, religion or non-belief with openness and cultural humility. In diagnosis, the possible effect of the person’s spiritual and religious perspective on health and well-being is taken into account. Adapting therapeutic goals and techniques to that perspective is therefore kept dependent on client consent.

title: Cultural context and worldview
summary: Considering belonging, support, commitment and constrained options without reducing one to another.
rawText: Cultural context and worldview Considering belonging, support, commitment and constrained options without reducing one to another. From label to experience Religious or cultural affiliation alone does not tell us what someone wants in counseling. This dossier proposes following a question about affiliation with inquiry into its lived meaning. The same community may be experienced as supportive and difficult. Keeping both possibilities open challenges a single, uniform notion of culture. Noticing metaphysical assumptions Hodge offers a theoretical discussion of metaphysical assumptions in mental health discourse. One reading question is whether practitioners treat their own position as the sole standard of neutrality. This is not a claim that all metaphysical views are clinically identical or that one is more effective. Commitment and available options A commitment can be meaningful while surrounded by difficult conditions. We propose distinguishing what the person wants to preserve, available options and the cost of acting differently. Staying or leaving is not predetermined as success. Respect for culture should not make concrete harm or safety needs invisible.

summary: The 2017 development study reports 29 items, five response categories and three dimensions, transcendence, harmony with nature and anomie. Overall internal consistency is reported as .886. originalTitle: Spiritual Well-Being: Conceptualization and Measurement
summary: Twenty items use six response categories to assess religious and existential wellbeing. Each subscale has ten items. The religious domain includes a relationship with God.
